lines: In his latest memo, Oaktree co-chair Howard Marks calls AI deeply consequential but highly unpredictable: the direction of progress is fairly foreseeable, while who profits, when, and by how much is largely unknowable.

He argues a winning AI investment thesis is unlikely because it must be right on many independent variables at once, from technology and competitive structure to capital availability, and warns that commoditization could hand most of the value to users rather than providers.

Marks says 'picks and shovels' data center bets are not a safe haven, citing fast hardware obsolescence, regulatory pushback and possible overbuilding, though he views infrastructure as more predictable than frontier labs.

He flags dangerous market concentration in a handful of AI-related stocks, and says massive, rate-insensitive AI capital demand and circular financing deals are reshaping credit markets and could push rates higher.
His prescription: stop seeking certainty, take calibrated risks, and anchor on the relationship between price and intrinsic value.
title: A Layman Thinks About AI
